From drone images to canopy measurements for each ridge¶

Summary

  • Problem: We need to measure potato plant growth from drone images. Potato plant growth is the target variable of a predictive model. The pipeline obtains one plant measurement for each ridge and each flight date from a drone image. This value is the average canopy for each plant.
  • Method: A classical computer-vision pipeline does three operations:
    1. It fits a grid to the ridges.
    2. It uses field markers to warp polygons between dates.
    3. It applies a color segmentation for each date.
  • Examination: A person examined the segmentation visually. The notebook shows random lots next to their masks. It also shows difficult cases.
  • Scope: This notebook uses one field and two flight dates. It imports the functions of the pipeline and does not copy them. helpers.py contains only small plot and load functions.

1. Problem and terms¶

A drone flies over the trial field on multiple days during the season. The purpose is to measure the ground area that the plants cover on each date. This measurement is separate for each plot in the field. Each plot contains plants from a different batch. This experiment observes 180 different batches.

Term Definition
Orthophoto A drone image mosaic with a correction to a top view. You can measure distances on it.
Ridge One column of potato plants inside a plot
Lot One trial plot. It has four adjacent ridge sections.
Canopy The ground area that leaves cover, in a top view
Average canopy The total canopy of a ridge, divided by its 6 plants, in cm² per plant
Plattegrond The layout table of the trial. It gives the location of each lot number in the field.

Import helpers first. This module selects the showcase configuration and limits the libraries to one thread.

2. Data¶

The data comes from two flights over one field:

  • Reference date: The lot polygons were made on this date.
  • Earlier date: This notebook uses this date to show how polygons move between dates.

The pipeline receives the images as NumPy arrays. The next cell opens these arrays as memory maps. For this reason, the notebook reads only the pixels that it uses.

In [3]:
images = {date: h.open_image(date) for date in h.DATES}

pd.DataFrame([{
    'date': date,
    'role': 'reference' if date == h.REFERENCE_DATE else 'aligned to reference',
    'height (px)': image.shape[0],
    'width (px)': image.shape[1],
    'file size (MB)': round(image.nbytes / 1e6),
} for date, image in images.items()])

The next figure shows the same part of the trial field on the two dates. It shows three data problems:

  • The light and the soil color are different.
  • The plants are at different growth stages.
  • The two images are not aligned. The same ground has different pixel coordinates on each date. Section 4.3 corrects this.
In [4]:
# The same ground on each date, as (x start, y start). The flights are not aligned,
# so the earlier window is offset by the transform fitted in section 4.3.
PORTION_SIZE = 1400
PORTION_START = {h.REFERENCE_DATE: (2000, 2150), h.OTHER_DATE: (2673, 3126)}

figure, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 5.6))
for ax, date in zip(axes, h.DATES):
    x0, y0 = PORTION_START[date]
    ax.imshow(images[date][y0:y0 + PORTION_SIZE, x0:x0 + PORTION_SIZE],
              extent=(x0, x0 + PORTION_SIZE, y0 + PORTION_SIZE, y0))
    ax.set(title=date, xlabel='x (pixels)')
axes[0].set_ylabel('y (pixels)')
figure.suptitle('Different light conditions on different dates')
plt.show()

Changes in the light are the reason that one color threshold is not sufficient. Hue is the color angle, in OpenCV units from 0 to 179.

In each histogram (after the next cell), the large peak on the left is the soil. The smaller peak on its right is the plants. The position and the width of the plant peak change between dates. For this reason, each date has its own hue band.

hist_analsis from Step 8 uses Otsu's method to calculate a possible lower bound. Here, it uses a sample of the image pixels. A person set the upper bound manually. Further steps in the pipeline refine the segmentation.

In [5]:
figure, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 5), sharey=True)
for ax, date in zip(axes, h.DATES):
    sample = np.array(images[date][::HISTOGRAM_STEP, ::HISTOGRAM_STEP])
    edges, density, _, otsu = hist_analsis(sample)
    low, high = h.hue_bounds(date)
    ax.bar(edges[:-1], density, width=edges[1] - edges[0], color='#8a9a5b')
    ax.axvline(otsu, color='k', ls=':', label=f'Otsu suggestion {otsu:.1f}')
    ax.axvspan(low, high, color='tab:green', alpha=0.2,
               label=f'stored band {low:.1f} to {high:.1f}')
    ax.set(title=date, xlabel='Hue (OpenCV units, 0-179)', xlim=(0, 90))
    ax.legend(frameon=False)
axes[0].set_ylabel('Probability density (per hue unit)')
figure.suptitle('Histogram of hue distribution on the two dates, later dates show more green cover')
plt.show()

3. Pipeline overview¶

The steps send data to each other through files on the disk. For this reason, you can run, examine and run again each step alone. The interactive steps are intentional. A person does Steps 3 and 5 once, on the reference date. A person does Steps 1, 2 and 8 for each date, and Step 6 for each other date. Steps 4, 7 and 9 are automatic.

In this notebook, the clicks from the interactive steps come from saved files. The notebook runs all other steps that it shows.

4. Pipeline steps¶

4.1 Lot boundaries on one ridge (Step 4)¶

Method. Short gaps with no plants separate the lots. Step 4 first applies a rough green filter and a morphological cleanup. It then reads the pixel values along three parallel lines on each ridge. A gap is a location where all three lines are empty.

Step 4 then compares the gaps with a grid that has equidistant gaps:

  • If a gap is less than 35% of one lot length from its expected position, Step 4 keeps the gap.
  • If not, Step 4 uses the expected position.

Reason. Plants grow across some gaps. For this reason, detection alone does not find all boundaries. The known plant pattern gives the other boundaries, and a person accepts the result in Step 5.

Step 4 usually runs one process for each ridge on the full image. One ridge in one process is sufficient to show the method.

In [7]:

4.2 Polygons on the reference date (Step 7)¶

Method. Each accepted grid cell has four ridges. Step 7 changes each cell into a lot polygon with 13 points. The trial layout gives the lot number of each polygon.

The next figure shows one part of the field two times. The left panel shows the gaps accepted in Step 5. The right panel shows the polygons that Step 7 makes from these gaps.

In [8]:

x0, y0 = PORTION_START[h.REFERENCE_DATE]
PORTION_X, PORTION_Y = (x0, x0 + PORTION_SIZE), (y0, y0 + PORTION_SIZE)
portion = images[h.REFERENCE_DATE][y0:y0 + PORTION_SIZE, x0:x0 + PORTION_SIZE]
gaps = np.vstack([h.accepted_gaps(quadrant) for quadrant in h.QUADRANTS])

figure, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 5.6), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for ax, title in zip(axes, ('Gaps accepted in Step 5', 'Lot polygons from these gaps')):
    ax.imshow(portion, extent=(*PORTION_X, PORTION_Y[1], PORTION_Y[0]))
    ax.set(title=title, xlabel='x (pixels)')
axes[0].set_ylabel('y (pixels)')
axes[0].plot(*gaps.T, ls='', color='r', marker='+', ms=10)
for polygon in reference_polygons.values():
    axes[1].plot(*polygon.T, color='yellow', lw=1)
axes[0].set(xlim=PORTION_X, ylim=PORTION_Y[::-1])
plt.show()

4.3 Polygon alignment across dates (Steps 6 and 7)¶

Reason. The pipeline makes the polygons one time, on the reference date, and a person examines these steps. Images from different flights are not aligned. For this reason, the pipeline must transform the polygons to the reference frame of the other dates. Red markers are planted at fixed locations in the field for this purpose.

Method. sort_markers puts the markers in the same sequence on each date. The top marker is first. The other markers follow, from the nearest to the farthest. A person makes sure that the markers match in Step 6.

The next figure shows the sequence numbers. The same number must identify the same physical marker on the two dates.

In [9]:
sorted_markers = {date: sort_markers(np.load(markers_path(h.FIELD, date)).astype(float))[0]
                  for date in h.DATES}

figure, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(11, 5.6), sharex=True)
for ax, date in zip(axes, h.DATES):
    ax.imshow(images[date][::OVERVIEW_STEP, ::OVERVIEW_STEP],
              extent=(0, images[date].shape[1], images[date].shape[0], 0))
    ax.plot(*sorted_markers[date].T, 'r+', ms=8)
    for number, (x, y) in enumerate(sorted_markers[date]):
        ax.annotate(number, (x, y), color='white', fontsize=8,
                    xytext=(3, 3), textcoords='offset points')
    ax.set_title(f'{date}: {len(sorted_markers[date])} markers')
    ax.set_ylabel('y (pixels)')
axes[1].set_xlabel('x (pixels)')
plt.show()

aff_transform then uses least squares to fit one transform to all marker pairs. This transform has four parameters: two for translation, one for rotation and one for scale. It is a similarity transform:

$$ \begin{pmatrix} x' \\ y' \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} t_x \\ t_y \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} a & -b \\ b & a \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} $$

  • $(x, y)$ is the position of a marker on the reference date, in pixels.
  • $(x', y')$ is the position of the same marker on the target date, in pixels.
  • $(t_x, t_y)$ is the translation, in pixels.
  • $a$ and $b$ have no unit. They give the scale $s=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ and the rotation $\theta=\operatorname{atan2}(b,a)$.

The same transform then warps all points of each polygon.

In [10]:
reference_points = sorted_markers[h.REFERENCE_DATE]
target_points = sorted_markers[h.OTHER_DATE]

warped_polygons = aff_transform(reference_polygons, reference_points, target_points)
np.save(polygons_path(h.FIELD, h.OTHER_DATE), warped_polygons)

In the image following the next cell, the top row shows the result without alignment. The polygon from the reference date is at its original coordinates on the earlier image, and it is fully outside its lot. The bottom row shows the same lot after alignment. The figure shows three lots that are far apart, because an error in rotation or scale increases toward the ends of the field.

A person examined the alignment visually in this way. For this examination, Step 7 saves an overlay of the warped polygons on each target image.

In [11]:
ALIGNMENT_LOTS = (1, 360, 720)  # first, middle and last lot number
target_image = images[h.OTHER_DATE]

figure, axes = plt.subplots(2, len(ALIGNMENT_LOTS), figsize=(11, 6.4))
for column, lot in enumerate(ALIGNMENT_LOTS):
    both = np.vstack((reference_polygons[lot], warped_polygons[lot]))
    x0, y0, x1, y1 = h.window_around(both, margin=100)
    crop = np.asarray(target_image[y0:y1, x0:x1])
    for row, (label, polygons, colour) in enumerate((
            ('not aligned', reference_polygons, 'tab:red'),
            ('aligned', warped_polygons, 'yellow'))):
        h.show_image(axes[row, column], crop, f'Lot {lot}, {label}')
        axes[row, column].plot(*(polygons[lot] - [x0, y0]).T, color=colour, lw=1.5)
plt.show()

4.4 Segmentation (Steps 8 and 9)¶

Method. The pipeline segments each ridge crop separately, in two parts:

  1. Hue band. The pipeline sets the pixels outside the stored hue band of the date to black. This removes most of the soil.
  2. Vegetation index. The pipeline combines three indices of the pixels that stay into one score for each pixel:

$$ F = 0.2\,\mathrm{BI} + 0.2\,\mathrm{HI} + 0.6\,\mathrm{ExG}, \qquad \mathrm{BI}=\sqrt{\tfrac{r^2+g^2}{2}},\quad \mathrm{HI}=\frac{2r-g-b}{g-b},\quad \mathrm{ExG}=2g-(r+b) $$

  • $r$, $g$ and $b$ are the red, green and blue values of a pixel (0–255).
  • BI is a brightness index.
  • HI is a hue index.
  • ExG is the excess-green index.

The pipeline calculates the mask in this sequence:

  1. It divides each index by its maximum in the crop.
  2. It combines the three indices into $F$.
  3. It divides $F$ by its maximum in the crop.
  4. It keeps the pixels above 0.45.
  5. It applies a 3×3 median filter to remove isolated pixels.

The median filter also fills very small holes. For this reason, a very small number of mask pixels are outside the hue band.

The next figure shows the four ridges of one lot together. The pixels that the pipeline keeps have their original color. All other pixels are black.

Parameters. Step 8 gives the hue bounds for each date. The weights and the 0.45 threshold are fixed constants in color_index_mask.

In [12]:
EXAMPLE_LOT = 360  # a lot from the middle of the field
polygons_by_date = {h.OTHER_DATE: warped_polygons, h.REFERENCE_DATE: reference_polygons}

figure, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(9, 8))
for row, date in zip(axes, h.DATES):
    stages = h.segmentation_stages(images[date], polygons_by_date[date][EXAMPLE_LOT], date)
    h.show_image(row[0], stages['original'], f'{date}: original')
    h.show_image(row[1], stages['after hue band'], 'After the hue band')
    h.show_image(row[2], stages['canopy mask'], 'After the canopy mask')
plt.show()

4.5 From pixels to area (Step 9)¶

The average canopy of each ridge is:

$$ A = \frac{n \cdot c}{P} $$

  • $A$ is the average canopy, in cm² per plant.
  • $n$ is the number of canopy pixels in the ridge polygon.
  • $c$ is the ground area of one pixel, in cm².
  • $P = 6$ is the number of plants in a ridge.

It was not possible to separate single plants in the images. For this reason, the pipeline measures the total canopy of the ridge and divides it by $P$.

The pipeline calculates $c$ from the image. The distance between ridges is 75 cm. For this reason, the mean ridge distance in pixels gives the size of one pixel.

In [13]:
area_per_pixel = {date: find_px_to_cm2_coeff(polygons_by_date[date], h.FIELD) for date in h.DATES}

pd.DataFrame({
    'pixel area c (cm²)': area_per_pixel,
    'pixel side (cm)': {date: np.sqrt(c) for date, c in area_per_pixel.items()},
}).round(3)

5. Visual inspection of the segmentation¶

Procedure. A person examined random lots visually. The display showed each lot in the original image, next to its segmented image. The next cells do this procedure again on the two dates, with a fixed seed.

Each right panel shows the pixels that the pipeline counts, on a black background. Soil in this panel is soil that the mask kept. Leaves that are only in the left panel are leaves that the mask did not find.

This notebook does not give accuracy scores. The examination is only visual.

In [17]:
NUMBER_OF_RANDOM_LOTS = 6
lot_numbers = sorted(reference_polygons)
random_lots = np.random.default_rng(SEED).choice(lot_numbers, NUMBER_OF_RANDOM_LOTS, replace=False)


def draw_lot_row(axes_row, lot: int, date: str) -> None:
    '''Draw one lot on one date: the original with its polygon, then the mask view.'''
    crop, outline = h.lot_crop(images[date], polygons_by_date[date][lot])
    kept = h.segmentation_stages(images[date], polygons_by_date[date][lot], date)['canopy mask']
    h.show_image(axes_row[0], crop, f'Lot {lot}, {date}')
    axes_row[0].plot(*outline.T, color='yellow', lw=0.8)
    h.show_image(axes_row[1], kept, 'Pixels kept')


print('Lots drawn with seed', SEED, ':', sorted(int(lot) for lot in random_lots))

Lots drawn with seed 2021 : [358, 427, 477, 542, 676, 716]
In [18]:
figure, axes = plt.subplots(NUMBER_OF_RANDOM_LOTS, 4, figsize=(9, 2.9 * NUMBER_OF_RANDOM_LOTS))
for row, lot in zip(axes, random_lots):
    draw_lot_row(row[:2], int(lot), h.OTHER_DATE)
    draw_lot_row(row[2:], int(lot), h.REFERENCE_DATE)
plt.show()

Difficult cases¶

Random lots seldom show the worst results. For this reason, simple rules on the measurements also select lots for examination. These rules only select the lots. They do not measure accuracy.

The canopy usually grows in the five days between these flights. For this reason, a ridge that shows a smaller canopy on the later date is possibly an error. The lowest values are also important to examine.

In [19]:
change = raw[h.REFERENCE_DATE].merge(raw[h.OTHER_DATE], on=['Lot number', 'Ridge'],
                                     suffixes=(' later', ' earlier'))
change['Change (cm² per plant)'] = change['Average canopy later'] - change['Average canopy earlier']
change = change.rename(columns={'Lot number': 'Lot'})

lowest = {date: int(raw[date].loc[raw[date]['Average canopy'].idxmin(), 'Lot number'])
          for date in h.DATES}
difficult_lots = {
    'largest apparent shrink': int(change.loc[change['Change (cm² per plant)'].idxmin(), 'Lot']),
    f'lowest canopy on {h.REFERENCE_DATE}': lowest[h.REFERENCE_DATE],
    f'lowest canopy on {h.OTHER_DATE}': lowest[h.OTHER_DATE],
}
print(f"{(change['Change (cm² per plant)'] < 0).sum()} of {len(change)} ridges appear to shrink; largest:")
print(change.nsmallest(1, 'Change (cm² per plant)')[['Lot', 'Ridge', 'Change (cm² per plant)']].round(1).to_string(index=False))
difficult_lots

    draw_lot_row(row[2:], lot, h.REFERENCE_DATE)

The rows show these cases:

  1. Stray vegetation (lot 226). On the earlier date, a large green object is at the edge of the lot. Five days later, the object is not there. It is possibly a weed, or an adjacent plant that was removed later. The object has the correct color, so the mask keeps it. For this reason, the canopy of the ridge is too high on that date. A method that uses only color cannot identify what a plant is. The polygon is the only spatial limit.
  2. Hard shadows (lot 714). On the later date, the plants cause dark shadows. Leaves in shadow are dark and possibly fail the color test. For this reason, the mask keeps mainly the leaves in sunlight, and the canopy value is probably too low. Shadows change with the light during each flight, so this effect is different between dates.
  3. Very small plants (lot 652). Early in the season, each plant covers only a few pixels. For this reason, a small boundary error around a plant is a large part of its measured area. The mask finds these plants, but the relative uncertainty is highest here.

6. Design selection: why a classical pipeline and not a deep segmentation model¶

Item Classical pipeline (this work) Deep segmentation model
Start requirements No training step. A person sets the bounds for each date in an interactive step. A training step and sufficient data for it
Interpretability You can read and explain each rule. The failure cases above have direct causes. You must examine the behavior of the model to find the cause of a failure.
Robustness across dates The hue bounds for each date give this. The cost is a manual step. The model must learn this across seasons and fields.
Weak points Color only: stray vegetation and shadows, as shown above It can possibly learn context, for example plant shape. This is its advantage.

I expect that a learned model can give the largest improvement on the cases in section 5. These cases also give a clear visual comparison between a learned model and this baseline.

7. Limitations and next steps¶

Known limitations of the code

  • The code calculates the vegetation indices on 8-bit values. An operation such as $r^2$ wraps around when the true value is more than 255. The code keeps this behavior, because the thresholds were set with it.
  • The mask threshold is relative to the highest score in each crop. For this reason, the threshold changes for each ridge and is not one absolute value.
  • The code contains fixed layout values: 30 lots for each ridge in Step 4, and 720 lots and 2,880 ridges in Step 9.
  • The geometry steps are still interactive for each field and season.

Recommended next steps

  • Examine deep-learning segmentation and compare it with this pipeline.
  • Add automated tests and continuous integration.
  • Make a package of the pipeline that installs and runs as one tool.
  • Monitor data drift across seasons.

8. Reproducibility¶

  • Environment: Python 3.10. showcase/requirements.txt gives the fixed versions.
  • Run: Go to the showcase/ folder. Then run jupyter nbconvert --to notebook --execute --inplace plant_pipeline_showcase.ipynb.
  • Data: The images are approximately 750 MB for each date. This is too large for git. Get the images from the Releases page of this repository, and put them in examples/S_2021_crops/. The saved results of the interactive steps are already in examples/S_2021/.
  • Output files: All output files go to showcase/outputs/. The notebook does not change examples/.
  • Random selection: SEED above sets the selection.
